paras: The lynching of John Riggins took place near Bainbridge, Decatur County, Georgia, on the evening of August 17, 1915, when searching parties shot to death a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman. After the woman identified him, his captors killed him with about 100 shots. The killing happened the same day as the lynching of Leo Frank, and a Black correspondent in the Savannah Tribune pointed to the contrast between the two cases.

According to the Dawson News, the alleged assault occurred on Monday afternoon, August 16, on a country road between Amsterdam and Attapulgus, where a woman driving a buggy was attacked. Wire reports described her as the wife of a tobacco planter, while a Bainbridge resident later called her a "northern woman." The Dawson News called it the first such assault known in the county's history and said the woman had been unconscious much of the time since.

Searching parties went out after the assault, and the Dawson News reported that several men were brought before the woman during the day and spared when she did not accuse them. Early on the night of August 17 the searchers captured Riggins and carried him before her, and she identified him. The Associated Press reported that "the mob quickly killed him with about 100 shots," and the Richmond Times-Dispatch called the killers "a posse of farmers."

Most reports gave Riggins's age as 63, but a longer AP version printed in the Keowee Courier said he was about 23 years old and had been in the community only a few days. A Bainbridge resident wrote that the man "confessed to the crime, and was executed immediately," a claim that appears in no news report.

No report of an inquest, arrests or a grand jury inquiry was found. The Savannah Tribune's Augusta correspondent wrote that the governor would offer the limit in rewards for Frank's lynchers, while "not one dollar" would be offered to find and punish the mob at Bainbridge.

White papers carried the story as a short Associated Press dispatch from Bainbridge on August 18, and several headlines stated the accusation as fact, such as the Milwaukee Leader's "Negro Who Assaulted Woman Slain by Mob" and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic's "Shoot to Death Black Who Assaulted White Woman." Other versions ran under "Another Georgia Lynching" and said only that Riggins was "accused of assaulting" the woman. A shorter version naming him as 63 went into weekly news digests from Iowa to Louisiana into late August. The first wire item, printed in the Washington Herald, reported that three men had been lynched at Amsterdam but admitted that no details had been received.

The Black press gave the lynching brief notice: the Indianapolis Freeman ran a special from Bainbridge, and the St. Louis Argus put a single line in its news column, both saying Riggins was "accused of attacking a woman." The Savannah Tribune's Augusta letter went further, calling the two lynchings part of "Georgia's shame" and observing that "the case at Bainbridge received only passing notice" beside the outcry over Frank. Its writer stressed that the Bainbridge victim "was simply charged with assault and had not had a trial."
The Bainbridge resident's letter, printed by the Milwaukee Leader on September 4, used the lynching to defend the killing of Frank, saying it showed that "Georgia protects the virtue of her women."

Accounts differ on Riggins's age, 63 in most papers and about 23 in one AP version, and on whether he was killed at Bainbridge or at Amsterdam, 14 miles away. The early report of three victims was not repeated in any later account.

reader.title: Lynching of John Riggins
bases: Searching parties or a posse captured John Riggins, who was accused of assaulting a woman, and shot him to death without a trial (A1, A2, A17).

Riggins was shot to death by 'searching parties' or 'a posse of farmers' firing about 100 shots after his accuser identified him (A1, A2, A5); he had no trial, and the killing was punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A17, A22).

The AP wire (A1, A4, A5), a separate Georgia report (A11), a Black-press special (A10), the Savannah Tribune's Augusta correspondent (A17) and a Bainbridge resident's letter (A22) agree that a Black man accused of assaulting a woman was lynched near Bainbridge on Aug. 17; only an early rumor of three victims (A3) differs.
